abstract: This talk will share Novartis' transformative journey from SAS to R, highlighting our challenges, experiences, and successes. We'll discuss strategies to leverage open-source resources effectively and share insights on contributing to the open-source community.

title: Introduction to R Implementation and Educational Initiatives for SAS Programmers
abstract: We are planning to transition our analytical tools from SAS to R in the near future. I will share information about the educational initiatives we are working on for the introduction of R.

title: Break
China: new region, new topics, new perspectives and new heights
abstract: In this panel discussion, colleagues from China explore strategies for overcoming timezone challenges in daily work, with a focus on maintaining a healthy work-life balance. Additionally, the discussion delves into the future of statistical programming, particularly the opportunities and challenges posed by AI. Beyond individual impacts, the discussion addresses how AI will reshape the broader industry. An intriguing intersection emerges when AI-driven productivity enhancements are shown to also benefit work-life balance by reducing workload pressures and allowing for more flexible, efficient workflows across different time zones.

title: Clinical Analysis Report and Visualization Ensemble in R (carver)
abstract: Very few industry-wide standards exist for clinical reporting, but open-source technologies are bridging this gap. This presentation introduces our R package and Shiny application, Carver (Clinical Analysis Report and Visualization Ensemble in R), which generates clinical submission-ready tables and graphs. An earlier version focusing on Adverse Events related reports was developed by our team in collaboration with Phuse, ASA and FDA. It is now expanded as an open-source Pfizer project, under spotlight of CDISC Open Source Alliance (COSA). This project references FDA Integrated TLF Guide, CDISC Guidelines and CDISC Standard Data.  carver  uses standardized functions to build multiple clinical reports – under domains like Adverse Events, Lab Findings and Demography in Therapeutic Areas like Vaccine and Oncology. In addition to templates to create static tables and figures, the modularized Shiny application can also be used to generate interactive plots – with a feature to drill down to patient-level analysis.  carver  uses packages from the tidyverse suite, plotly, ggsurvfit, shiny, shinydashboard, shinyBS etc. For tables, we built a wrapper around Flextable package to dynamically fit a submission-ready format. The R functions are unit-tested, use tidy principles and CI/CD workflows were implemented. We aim for  carver  to be used for regulatory submissions and for clinical review. Another potential outcome could be to embed study data within a Shiny Dashboard and include it in clinical submission-package. We are seeking collaborators to expand its reporting capabilities across the pharma industry.

title: Break
Automation of reporting statistical results with R (mocktables, summary tables, result narrations)
abstract: For one who works with programming, working on word documents such as creating tables, adjusting spaces, fonts seems to be tiring. In the pharma domain, statisticians are involved in one such task of building mock shells for tables and replicating the same table structure (using programming software) to report statistical results. Statisticians are also required to provide statistical narratives for key results, which involves copying numerical values from summary tables and manually crafting the narrative - another time-consuming job. Many pharmaceutical companies have developed their own R libraries, some of which are available in the public domain. However, the output formats (i.e., the class of output objects) from these libraries are often not flexible and difficult to adapt to specific end-user requirements.  This abstract proposes a solution to these challenges using R by 1. Creating Custom R Functions (Macros) for table layout We propose building R functions that can generate table mock shells, which can later be reused to report statistical outputs. For example, a function like `fun_demo_tab` could be used to create a mock table for demographic data to be included in a TLF (Tables, Listings, and Figures) mock shell. The same function could then be reused to present the statistical summary of demographic data in the final report.  2. Automating Statistical Narration We suggest developing an R macro along with RMarkdown that can automatically extract numerical values from summary tables and integrate them into a predefined narrative framework. This would significantly reduce the time statisticians spend on this task, cutting it down from hours to just a few seconds.

title: Customize and Generate Clinical Study Report (CSR) document using {quarto}
abstract: In the pharmaceutical industry, TFLs can be generated through programming to support the final clinical study report. However, by referring to the TFL results, the medical writer needs to manually transcribe or copy/paste the outputs into the CSR. This entire process can consume several months, depending on the complexity of the study and regulatory requirements. To overcome this difficulty, we suggest using  quarto , which can derive descriptions, narratives, inline tables, figures, etc., for the CSR. In this session, we will discuss the rationale and feasibility of using such a tool, and example solutions will be provided.

title: Exploring interactive analytics with teal: supporting efficient communication in clinical science
abstract: In the near future, we would like to use teal to conduct interactive analysis and to realize efficient communication with clinical development menbers. We will share an overview of the project, consisting of biostatisticians and statistical programmers, and future prospects.

title: {whirl} – An Open-Source R package for Program Logs
abstract: Following, the first R-based submission from Novo Nordisk an internal journey began to give back to the open-source community. Novo Nordisk has developed several internal packages to support the infrastructure behind executing clinical trials in R, and now one of the first pieces are ready to be open-sourced.  In this presentation we’ll take you down the long and winding road of going from inner-sourced packages to open-sourced packages and reveal  whirl  which is our new open-source R package for executing scripts and producing GxP compliant logs when conducting clinical trials.   whirl  is an alternative to existing packages such as  logrx  and  logr  and is to be included as Novo Nordisk' first contribution to the pharmaverse.  The advantages of  whirl  are the support of multiple languages, and the html-based log reports, offering users a comprehensive overview of their processes.

title: Opening Remarks
Responsive Regulation of AI in Drug Development
abstract: Over the past few decades, the volume of data available to support drug and biological product development have increased substantially. These increases in data volume were also accompanied by an expansion in data diversity with data originating from disparate sources including biologic data, pharmacological data, and clinical data (e.g., imaging, electronic health records, and digital health technologies). This growth in data volume and complexity combined with cutting-edge computing power and methodological advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have the potential to transform how drugs and biological products are developed, manufactured, and utilized. Concurrent with these technological advancements, FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) have seen an exponential increase in the number of drug submissions using AI components, with over 200 submissions reported in 2023 compared to only 1 in 2016. These submissions traverse the drug product life cycle from drug discovery to postmarket safety monitoring and cut across a range of therapeutic areas. In general, the application of AI in these submissions aims to improve the efficiency of drug discovery and our understanding of the efficacy and safety of specific treatments. The diverse uses of AI in these submissions highlight the need for an adaptive regulatory assessment of benefits and risks and emphasizes the importance of adopting a risk-based approach for establishing and evaluating the credibility of an AI model output for a particular context of use.

title: Break
Harnessing CDISC’s Emerging Analysis Results Datasets Standard with the {cards} and {gtsummary} Packages
abstract: The CDISC Analysis Results Data (ARD) Model is an emerging standard for encoding statistical analysis summaries in a machine-readable format. Its primary objective is to streamline the processes of automation, ensuring reproducibility, promoting reusability, and enhancing traceability.  The newly released  cards  R package, a collaborative effort in the Pharmaverse including Roche, GSK, and Novartis, offers a variety of functions for ARD generation. These range from basic univariate summaries like means and tabulations to complex multivariable summaries encompassing regression models and statistical tests.  While  cards  calculates statistics and stores them in a structured object, it cannot present those results; this, however, is where the  gtsummary  R package shines. The  gtsummary  package offers a modular framework to construct summary tables. It won the American Statistical Association’s 2021 award for Innovation in Statistical Programming and Analytics, and also won first place in Posit BPC’s Table Contest’s pharmaceutical track. The  gtsummary  package was recently refactored to utilize  cards  as its backend, which will allow users to both extract an ARD object from a  gtsummary  table and use an ARD object to construct a  gtsummary  table.   Our recent experience utilizing the  cards  and  gtsummary  R packages  to prepare a health authority filing highlighted the benefits of using ARDs, including improved automation, reproducibility, reusability, and traceability. We believe that this approach will become increasingly essential for ensuring the quality and efficiency of clinical trial reporting.

title: Sample Size or Power Calculations for Trial Design with Hierarchical Endpoints - an R Shiny App
abstract: Win measures, such as win ratio, win odds, net benefit, and desirability of outcome ranking (DOOR), have become popular approaches for the analysis of hierarchical endpoints in clinical studies. For trial design with these win measures based on hierarchical endpoints, sample size and power calculations are often based on simulation studies that can be cumbersome.  Existing sample size and power formulas require investigators to specify clinically significant and meaningful magnitude of win measures and probability of ties that are difficult to elicit based on prior published literature or preliminary data.  To overcome these difficulties, we express the win measures as function of marginal win measures that are readily available under independence assumption and this provides a novel way to specify a meaningful and justifiable magnitude of win measures and the magnitude of probability of ties. We built a very flexible R shiny app (https//duke-som.shinyapps.io/Hierarchical_Endpoints/) that can quickly compute a sample size with a given power or compute a power with a given sample size for any clinical trial design with two groups for any number of hierarchical endpoints, any type of endpoints (time to event, counts, binary, or ordinal), and any order of hierarchy of these endpoints.

title: Optimising Team Collaboration with Shiny
abstract: In the fast moving Pharmaceutical industry, efficiency between teams is key. This was at the forefront of our minds when launching our shiny application GLITTER, built to take data input from our programming teams and produce formatted word documents for our medical writers.  However, when launching our application we experienced some teething problems. Our data inputs were not always fit for purpose, leading to time consuming communication loops between the two teams to bug fix and reach the desired outcome.  In this talk, I will discuss how through some small tweaks to our shiny application, we were able to produce a companion tool - GLITTER for programmers. This not only empowered our programmers to validate their own inputs, but also reduced unnecessary feedback cycles between teams. This showcases that the key to effective tooling often lies within existing code, it's just a matter of rethinking its application.

title: R Package Validation Framework: Docker Integration
abstract: With the rapid adoption of R in the pharmaceutical industry, the topic of R package validation has become a focal point of discussion. Ensuring that these packages perform in a reproducible and reliable manner is not just important, but essential for maintaining the integrity of data analysis and regulatory compliance. Across the industry, numerous professionals have shared their methodologies for validating open-source R packages, each contributing valuable insights into best practices and common challenges. Despite the wealth of shared knowledge, one area remains relatively unexplored the validation of R packages within Docker images. Docker, a platform that enables the creation and deployment of applications in isolated containers, offers a powerful tool for ensuring consistency across different computing environments. By encapsulating R packages and their dependencies within Docker images, we can achieve a high level of reproducibility and portability. This talk aims to delve into this niche yet significant topic and provide a guide to tailoring your validation process to leverage Docker for R package validation, enhancing the reproducibility and reliability of computational results in the pharmaceutical industry.

title: Break
Leveraging Artificial Intelligence in R for Predicting Drug Behavior
abstract: Discover how AI models can revolutionize drug development towards personalized applications, by predicting drug behavior while integrating multiple data sources including formulation attributes, manufacturing process parameters, and in-vitro experimental data of pharmaceutical products.

title: Apply machine learning methods to retinal clinical data in R
abstract: Our objective was to develop predictive models for fibrosis, which is a crucial symptom response in the retinal health, using baseline characteristics and to identify key biomarkers associated with fibrosis progression. We utilized a comprehensive dataset that includes demographic information, ophthalmic exams (such as OCT and fluorescein angiography), and treatment details from the clinical trials. The data preparation involved integrating multiple datasets to create a robust training set. We employed various machine learning techniques, including ensemble methods (XGBoost, Random Forest), Support Vector Machine (SVM), and partial least squares regression, to develop our models. The models' performance was evaluated based on sensitivity, specificity, and area under the ROC curve (AUC).  In the work, all results are done in R markdown which integrate the code, comments and result. Besides, data manipulation is fitted with clinical standard to display demographic statistics table. We hope the result from R could be used in clinics and also create a package for other users to run the machine learning methods as a standardized way in the future.

title: Introducing WebR to TLG Catalog
abstract: This talk will introduce the integration of the WebR framework into the TLG Catalog - a catalog of Tables, Listings, and Graphs outputs for clinical reporting. WebR, which ports R into WebAssembly (WASM), enables compiled R code to run directly on websites, making the TLG Catalog more accessible and efficient, especially for learning and experimentation. The presentation will include an introduction to the TLG Catalog, a brief overview of WebR technology, a live demo, and a discussion on the integration's impact.

title: Break
Why Cant I Print This?: Adventures In Creating Interactive Safety Reports
abstract: For Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) reports, Biogen has moved from static, SAS-based reports to interactive R Markdown reports that allow users to immerse themselves in the data during review. While several stakeholders have welcomed this new way of working, this change has not been without challenges. This talk will go over the concept and execution of these reports, the strategies to overcome these challenges, and the benefits that switching to a web-based output has given to the organization.

title: Enhancing Late-Stage Process Development with R
abstract: The value that R brings to clinical reporting is well established, and this has been the key factor in securing R's position within the pharma industry. However, as effective data collection, curation, and aggregation have increased across functions within the pharma industry over the past years, real opportunities have emerged to leverage R's ecosystem across the development pipeline. For the past five years I have been working as a data scientist supporting late-stage process development teams, and I'll use this talk to describe some successful applications of R to common process development challenges in data analysis and reporting, as well as some areas where further improvement is needed.

title: Streamlining Data Edit Checks via Interactive Document
abstract: Interactive reports enable users to perform data discovery and analysis and provides a more engaging and dynamic experience compared with static reports. However, presenting interactive reports with Shiny or Dash requires the use of an external server which can be costly and time consuming. Interactive reports using Quarto or Rmarkdown can be a valuable alternative to create accessible, user-friendly reports that provide comparative use to more server intensive applications without the expense.

title: DuckDB and duckplyr: An in-process database management system in your R script
abstract: DuckDB is an open-source analytical database management system with clients for several languages, including R. DuckDB offers the functionality of a database system, including high performance, persistence and full SQL support. At the same time, DuckDB has a small footprint with no dependency on an external server it is trivial to deploy using the library(duckdb) call. DuckDB also has deep integrations into client libraries such as dplyr using the duckplyr package. In this talk, I explain how DuckDB achieves its high performance, demonstrate its performance through a live demo and showcase its R integrations.

title: Using git for a multilingual approach to trial activities
abstract: This presentation explores the innovative use of Git to facilitate a multilingual approach in clinical trial execution at Novo Nordisk. It highlights the transition from SAS to R, driven by the need for improved efficiency and code reusability. The presentation details the setup of a new version control system, statistical computing environment, and the integration of Git and CI pipelines to manage and execute programs in multiple languages. It emphasizes the benefits of Git, including enhanced traceability, new review processes, and intelligent branch management. The future vision includes seamless orchestration of programs, independent of language and manual execution, ensuring a unified and efficient workflow.

title: Implementation of {teal} Shiny apps in DMC activity
abstract: There have been two pilot studies discussing submission to the FDA through R Shiny. With such applications, an efficient and interactive review can now be conducted. While most of the applications focus on using R Shiny applications within an organization for internal review of compounds, R Shiny packages such as  teal  can be implemented for DMC activities. Interactive dashboards using R to perform analysis, which can be inclusive to study-specified analysis and endpoint, such as using  rtables ,  tern , and  teal . Moreover, such an approach can provide downloadable/portable files for further reference. In this session, we will discuss the feasibility of such an application into DMC activity.

title: Gearing our industry Statisticians up for Software success : A phase1b journey
abstract: Trial statisticians write software and are well placed to contribute to analytical solutions that inform business and clinical decision making. Early conversations about incorporating software engineering competence in a trials statistician’s (Sabanés Bové, 2023) already impressive toolbox have started to emerge with the use of the common language of R. I share my personal experience about the actions and attitudes to achieve a state-of-art solution called phase1b and highlight good software engineering principles and ways of working. The package phase1b (Yeo et al, 2024)  is a flexible toolkit that evaluates efficacy and futility analysis within the Bayesian framework for early Oncology trials. The R package informs decision making on whether the drug of concern warrants further investment. Since the evaluation of the efficacy and futility impacts business and clinical decisions in pharma, it is advantageous that the industry strives to understand and create the conditions for more Software success such as the phase1b.

Using Shiny to Clearly Present Clinical Results with CDISC-Compliant Dataset
abstract: I am going to demonstrate how to use Shiny to effectively present clinical results using CDISC-compliant datasets, such as SDTM. The main points of the presentation are as follows  1. Using Shiny to present key domains and combine information from multiple domains within clinical datasets.  2. Presenting specific group or individual information with Shiny, enhancing the clarity and visualization of clinical results.  3. Ensuring that the Shiny app is user-friendly for non-programming users, enabling efficient data exploration and monitoring.

title: Exploring Shiny for Quality Compliance Checks of Clinical Programming Deliverables
abstract: The use of interactive web applications has become increasingly prominent in various industries due to their ability to enhance user experience and streamline processes. In clinical programming, ensuring the quality and compliance of deliverables is paramount to uphold regulatory standards and safeguard patient safety. The Shiny application is effectively used for creating interactive web application that facilitate quality compliance checks in clinical programming frameworks. At Novo Nordisk, a user friendly Shiny application has been developed to read various file formats like SAS, R, TXT, PNG and HTML, perform various compliance checks , compare different versions of Tables, Figures, Listings to highlight the issues and generate summary reports for review. Integrating Shiny into the quality compliance process in clinical programming presents a robust solution to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of quality assurance.

title: Break
Transforming EDC Data into Practical Insights: The Power of a One-Click R-Shiny App
abstract: In our daily study practice, we identified the need for a concise and straightforward tool to help study teams extract significant information from the latest EDC raw data. However, study teams often find themselves overwhelmed by the vast amount of EDC data and overly complex data review tools. To address this, we developed a one-click R-Shiny App that bridges EDC data directly to actionable outputs, enabling the detection of critical signals related to data quality. The goal of this one-click R-Shiny App is to resolve the following challenges 1. Provide a global dashboard that accommodates all company-level studies. 2. Detect patterns between the overall population and the China subgroup in safety data, end-of-treatment, end-of-study, protocol deviations, and biomarker sample collection. 3. Extract the most critical exception listings. 4. Address the issue of variable names lacking direct access to variable labels.

title: {BayesCVI} A Bayesian cluster validity index with medical applications
abstract: The Bayesian Cluster Validity Index (BCVI) is a new concept that directly applies the Bayesian framework to CVIs. This connection is unique and has not been explored before in the literature. In this talk, we introduce BCVI, which can be used in conjunction with any existing CVIs, particularly advantageous for users who have prior knowledge of the expected number of clusters in their datasets. We will explore the BCVI concept in depth, demonstrating its integration with the BayesCVI (https//CRAN.R-project.org/package=BayesCVI) available on CRAN and applying it to diverse real-world applications such as health science data and MRI image brain tumor detection.

title: Break
Breaking down cognitive barriers for new members to your project and your future self
abstract: At Appsilon, we focus on helping diverse teams build Shiny apps to solve their problems. Over time, we've observed common project patterns that hinder onboarding and create barriers to productive contributions. In this discussion, we will detail these patterns and provide strategies to mitigate them, supported by case studies of projects that have successfully overcome these challenges. These barriers include a lack of documentation, complex setup processes, insufficient dependency management, poor code organization, and inadequate testing, among others. At first, these topics may seem more closely related to the responsibilities of professional developers rather than members working within business lines. However, it becomes much easier to address these issues with access to some helpful tools. We will discuss these tools and how to implement them in your project with minimal effort. Defining such standards will ensure that future projects and teams work seamlessly and effectively.

title: R, Docker and Nextflow – Building the stable Data pipeline
abstract: Stability of statistical results is essential in drug development. Many research groups develop in-house pipelines for data processing and analysis, incorporating with R packages, internal computations, and even integrate with other language like Python. However, untracked tool updates can lead to result variability or pipeline failures.  At Silence Therapeutics, we've implemented a three-tiered approach to ensure result reliability, reproducibility, and robustness  1. Automated semantic versioning Tracks changes in our data pipeline when internal or external developers update functions. 2. Docker containerization Ensures consistent environments for reproducible results. 3. Nextflow integration Enables scalable execution of our containerized pipelines on AWS cloud.  This comprehensive system provides a solid foundation for our drug development efforts by maintaining pipeline integrity and result consistency.

title: Introducing openstatsware: Who we are and what we build together
abstract: In this talk, we would like to introduce openstatsware, an official working group of ASA BIOP as well as EFSPI/PSI. The working group has a primary objective to engineer R packages that implement important statistical methods, and a secondary objective to develop and disseminate best practices for engineering high-quality open-source statistical software. We will talk about what R packages we have been developing and what we have done to disseminate the best practices, as well as our long-term perspective and next steps.

title: Building a reproducible workflow using {targets}
abstract: Reproducibility and efficiency are critical in data analysis workflows, particularly in complex projects with multiple interdependent tasks. The  targets  package in R offers a robust solution for orchestrating reproducible and scalable workflows. By defining and managing a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of tasks,  targets  ensures that each step in the workflow is executed in the correct order and only when necessary, saving time and computational resources. In this presentation, we will demonstrate how to build a reproducible workflow using  targets . We will explore the core features of the package, including target definition, dependency management, and automated pipeline execution. Through practical examples, we will show how  targets  can be integrated with other R packages to handle data processing, modeling, and visualization seamlessly. Additionally, we will discuss practical tips for maintaining workflows, ensuring they remain efficient and manageable as project complexity grows. Whether you are new to  targets  or looking to enhance your workflow automation, this session will provide valuable insights and practical techniques to elevate your data analysis projects.

title: Whats the return on investment from open sourcing?
Building living apps in Shiny for better modeling insights and outcomes
abstract: Shiny is not just a tool for rapidly exploring and visualizing data. It can also be leveraged as a highly effective framework for interacting with models. In this talk, we'll explore how Shiny can be used to customize simulations and run them dynamically. By providing stakeholders more control over model decisions, data scientists can develop deeper partnerships and engagement. This approach helps to build a common language, share domain knowledge, and ultimately find practical solutions for the challenges at hand.

title: Opening Remarks
Accelerating GSK’s Open-Source Journey with Gen AI
abstract: This presentation provides an insightful exploration of GSK's innovative journey in integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into biostatistics. It begins with the strategic introduction of LLMs to users, progressing through to the pioneering LLM experiments aimed at automating our reporting pipeline. We will delve into the crucial considerations for successfully introducing LLMs to a biostatistics audience, sharing key insights learned from our experience. The presentation culminates with a forward-looking discussion on the evolving roles within the organization as the use of LLMs expands, highlighting GSK's commitment to embracing change and leading the way in technological advancements.

title: Break
abstract: Whilst the number of multilingual programming teams for clinical study work has been growing, so has the issue of cross-language data compatibility. If care is not taken we risk antiquated or inadequate formats becoming the de facto standard, or worse yet a return to complete interoperability from the use of language specific data formats (Rds, Pickle, etc). This presentation will discuss a number of open data formats, with a comparative analysis of their strengths and weaknesses. In particular, this presentation will introduce and recommend Apache Parquet, a high performance binary data format that comes with client libraries for most popular analytical programming languages as well as integration into many popular tools and databases. Finally, the talk will touch on our experiences and challenges of trying to integrate Apache Parquet within our data analysis workflows at Roche.

title: An arrow towards the future: a critical look at data formats for clinical reporting
Explore Real-World hospital Electronic Health Records data with ggehr
abstract: This talk will introduce the integration of the WebR framework into the TLG Catalog - a catalog of Tables, Listings, and Graphs outputs for clinical reporting. WebR, which ports R into WebAssembly (WASM), enables compiled R code to run directly on websites, making the TLG Catalog more accessible and efficient, especially for learning and experimentation. The presentation will include an introduction to the TLG Catalog, a brief overview of WebR technology, a live demo, and a discussion on the integration's impact.

title: Teal Builder - The Fastest Way to Build Reproducible Teal Apps
abstract: This session will introduce Teal Builder, a powerful Shiny application designed to simplify the creation of Teal apps without requiring users to write any R code. The presentation will cover the purpose and functionality of Teal Builder, demonstrate how to run the app locally, and provide a live demonstration of its capabilities. Teal Builder not only streamlines the process of building Teal apps but also provides a platform for generalizing certain internal statistical methods and processes into reusable modules to be used by more studies.  Teal Builder offers a user-friendly interface that guides users through data selection from multiple sources, module selection and compatibility validation based on the selected data. The app generates reproducible R code for running the Teal app or deploying it to Posit Connect, making the process efficient and accessible. It fulfills the unmet need of having an interactive data display for all studies, promoting Teal and R/Shiny adoption and usage to new R and non-R users.  Teal Builder comprises three R packages teal.builder, teal.builder.modules, and teal.builder.checks. The teal.builder package contains functions for running the Shiny app and serves as the entry point for most users. The teal.builder.modules package offers a collection of predefined module specifications, including module names, descriptions, data requirements, and reproducible code. The teal.builder.checks package provides functions to ensure user data adheres to specifications, offering detailed feedback when necessary.  During the demonstration, we will walk through the user journey of building a Teal app with Teal Builder. We'll showcase how a complex app for exploring ADaM datasets, which typically requires around 500 lines of code, can be generated in just a few minutes. This session will highlight the efficiency and user-friendliness of Teal Builder, making it an invaluable tool for those working with Teal apps.

title: ramnog: R package suite for automating statistical analyses
abstract: Health Technology Assessment (HTA) involves evaluating the relevance and value of health technologies, such as drugs, within health care systems. Supporting this process from a biostatistical perspective requires a different mindset and distinct analytical methods compared to those used in regulatory submissions.  One approach to HTA is the German AMNOG process, which requires extensive data slicing to produce the necessary statistical material. This approach necessitates significant programming and orchestration effort, especially when following a traditional "one output - one program" methodology.  Compounding the challenge, the EU's joint initiative to streamline the HTA process across Europe, known as EU HTA, allows all member countries to bring forward similar individual requirements. This implies a significant increase in number of data slices and analyses required and a substantial workload for statistical programmers in the future. However, many of these analyses are repetitive and suitable for automation.  At Novo Nordisk we are involved in the HTA-R workstream under openstatsware where we are developing an open source ecosystem of R packages called  ramnog  to address the current challenges of AMNOG and the future demands of EU HTA. The goal is to automate repetitive tasks, allowing our colleagues more time to focus on complex analyses.  In our presentation, we will guide you through the practical aspects of specifying an analysis required for a typical AMNOG output and demonstrate how the package runs the analysis. Additionally, we will provide a technical overview of the ecosystem, detailing the roles and considerations of the individual components.

title: Break
Building Rome in a month: How open-source technologies empower small pharma
abstract: Traditionally, small pharmaceutical or biotech companies, often limited by resources, tend to rely on FSPs or CROs for statistical programming and analytics support. The emergence and maturation of enterprise-caliber open-source software and tools present new and transformative opportunities for these organizations by helping to enhance data accessibility, streamline analysis workflows, and foster collaborative innovation. However, building these types of infrastructure within small pharma involves navigating budget constraints, limited IT resources, stakeholder buy-in and the need for specialized expertise. Overcoming these challenges requires strategic planning, prioritization, and training. This presentation will delve into the practical aspects and lessons learned from our experience of building up open-source technologies, such as the Posit computing environment, from scratch within the Clinical Development department at Recursion. By tackling these infrastructural hurdles, the integration of open-source toolsets has significantly improved our data analysis capabilities, accelerating drug development and positioning our company at the forefront of pharmaceutical innovation.

title: Roche’s first end-to-end R submission
abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of pharmaceutical development, Roche showcases the use of open source R in the regulatory submission process. In this presentation we will share a pioneer experience of end-to-end R submission for a new drug application to FDA, EMA and NMPA.  The successful end-to-end NDA submission using R packages, the majority being open source packages (from pharmaverse), not only demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of leveraging such a powerful tool in the regulatory realm but also sets a precedent for its wider adoption in the pharmaceutical industry.

title: Our R-Based Submissions: A 1-year follow-up, Lessons Learned, and Future Strategies
abstract: In this presentation we will share our journey towards scaling our R-usage from our first submission, and the feedback we have received from authorities in doing so.  We will highlight our strategic direction and what role open-source will play for Novo Nordisk in future submissions.

title: Break
Piloting into the Future: Publicly Available R-based Submissions to the FDA
abstract: Recent years have seen a significant shift towards the adoption of open-source software like R by statisticians and analysts in both industry and regulatory agencies. This trend offers immense benefits, including cutting-edge statistical tools, interactive dashboard packages like Shiny, and adaptability to modern data science trends. Despite these advantages, the pharmaceutical industry's broader adoption of R for drug submissions has been limited. To address this, the R Consortium R Submissions Working Group (RCRSWG) aims to demonstrate that an R-based submission can be successfully reviewed by the FDA.  By May 2024, the RCRSWG completed three pilot submissions and received response letters from the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), marking a significant milestone. These submissions are the first publicly available packages that use open-source languages.  This presentation will share highlights from May 2024, where three pilot submissions from RCRSWG were completed successfully with response letters from the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), marking a significant milestone. These submissions are the first publicly available packages that use open-source languages.   Additionally, we will provide an update on the ongoing work in Pilot 4 as well as explore the potential of R in regulatory submissions and the RCRSWG's efforts to improve R-based clinical trial submissions.   All materials are available on the R Consortium's GitHub page, showcasing our commitment to transparency and innovation in regulatory submissions.

title: Panel discussion on open source submissions
Opening Remarks
Christina Fillmore’s Keynote (APAC Replay)
abstract: This presentation provides an insightful exploration of GSK's innovative journey in integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) into biostatistics. It begins with the strategic introduction of LLMs to users, progressing through to the pioneering LLM experiments aimed at automating our reporting pipeline. We will delve into the crucial considerations for successfully introducing LLMs to a biostatistics audience, sharing key insights learned from our experience. The presentation culminates with a forward-looking discussion on the evolving roles within the organization as the use of LLMs expands, highlighting GSK's commitment to embracing change and leading the way in technological advancements.

title: Discussion of Christina Fillmore’s Keynote
Break
The use case of Copilot into open-source programming
abstract: Recently, it is a common practice to use R to develop functionality or Shiny application for statistical analysis or reporting. With the development of GenAI and integration of Copilot into RStudio/Posit Workbench, programmer can utilize such tool to improve their development efficiency. In this session, we will explore some use cases of Copilot in daily statistical activity and introduce how to use Copilot efficiently.

title: Creating a Doctor Network using R and Graph Databases
abstract: In this session, we will describe how we are leveraging R to build datasets from different sources (internal and external) to create a network of doctor-related activities within a graph database system. We also use the Cypher query language to create use cases from there.

title: Break
How do we, statistical programmers in pharmaceutical companies, use R? - Japan Experiences Panel
The R Shiny app TNfinder for tumor-normal expression analysis
abstract: We developed a Shiny application to deliver fast and flexible tumor-normal gene expression analysis based on TCGA and GTEx data. Compared to the widely-used public tool GEPIA, TNfinder offers more tailored functions including gene signature analysis, T-N cutoff evaluation, population estimation, tumor-specific marker detection, and enhanced visualization options. This app provides biologists with a convenient tool to perform expression analysis in oncology target identification and assessment.

title: Break
R(omeo) and Julia - A Love Story by openstatsware
PCA in R: A CAMIS Working Group Initiative in Pharma
abstract: CAMIS is a PHUSE working group whose goal is to find several discrepancies between statistical analysis methods using various software. The speaker intends to delve into the fundamentals of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and its applications using R. In the pharmaceutical and Healthcare Industry, the vast amount of patient data poses a significant challenge for researchers and clinicians seeking to identify meaningful patterns and relations among the variables. PCA provides an effective approach by reducing dimensionality and uncovering underlying structures in complex datasets.

title: Closing Remarks
Selected examples on how to scale-up computations in R (e.g. by using HPC)
No code data analysis with blockr
R Validation Hub Risk Tools Developer Day
Building the Future of Data Apps: LLMs Meet Shiny
abstract: When we think of LLMs (large language models), usually what comes to mind are general purpose chatbots like ChatGPT or code assistants like GitHub Copilot. But as useful as ChatGPT and Copilot are, LLMs have so much more to offer—if you know how to code. In this demo Garrick will explain LLM APIs from zero, and have you building and deploying custom LLM-empowered data workflows and apps in no time.

title: Break
Interactive and Instant: GenAI-driven Creation of Clinical Trial Applications
abstract: Building exploratory analysis dashboards for clinical trials traditionally requires considerable expertise, extensive time, and deep familiarity with specialized frameworks such as R/Shiny and  teal . In this talk, we share our experience exploring how Generative AI can significantly streamline this process. We will present a tool we developed, powered by Claude Code, that enables biostatisticians and clinical researchers to effortlessly create and immediately preview R/Shiny applications tailored for exploratory clinical data analysis using  teal . Throughout our journey, we experimented with various GenAI-driven solutions, including code editors integrated with AI assistance tools (e.g., GitHub Copilot), and approaches leveraging MCP servers. Our current implementation is an interactive AI-powered chat interface designed to simplify the application-building experience, providing users with immediate application previews, and reducing both development complexity and the learning curve associated with the  teal  package. We will demonstrate how GenAI-driven solutions can empower users with limited programming backgrounds to rapidly build effective exploratory analysis dashboards, discuss challenges encountered, and highlight insights gained through our iterative development process.

title: Building an AI Pair Programmer for ADaM
abstract: At Novo Nordisk, we seek to deliver medicines more effectively and efficiently by leveraging the capabilities of Generative AI to accelerate our processes. We want to support our clinical trial programming activities with AI tools and coding assistants, scaling the output and impact of our statistical programmers. Delivering a product in this space poses numerous scientific and technical challenges What is the right context to expose to an externally hosted model? What workflow will best support our employees and leverage their domain knowledge? What design choices will best integrate with our existing IT landscape? In this presentation we will discuss the features we built and experimentation conducted to tackle the above questions, and how we are integrating Generative AI into the ADaM programming processes. The work presented represents a joint venture between our Biometrics and AI & Analytices organization and in collaboration with Microsoft’s Industry Solutions Engineering team.

title: Enabling GenAI Capabilities for Statistical Programmers
abstract: At Pfizer, we are committed to enhancing the capabilities of our statistical programmers by leveraging GenAI. Our goal is to empower R users with AI tools to streamline workflows and boost productivity. We have integrated GitHub Copilot within the RStudio IDE, resulting in significant time savings and improved documentation. Additionally, we introduced the voxr package, which simplifies interaction with our internal Vox LLM API, enabling tasks such as text generation and sentiment analysis using state-of-the-art language models. This presentation will showcase the features we’ve developed, and the experimentation conducted to enhance productivity and LLM model interaction across the organization. We have observed significant time savings driven by improved debugging, documentation, and custom training. This presentation will discuss the features we have built, and the development and testing conducted to address key challenges, such as integration with external open-source efforts, ensuring responsible use, and improving performance by providing the right context. By expanding access to these tools and providing custom training, we aim to create a more empowered and productive user base.

title: R/Pharma - GenAI in Pharma - Hangout
Maximizing LLM Potential: How Data Structure and Context Drive Quality Insights
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) promise to revolutionize clinical data analysis but struggle with messy, imperfect datasets common in drug development research. This presentation demonstrates how the inclusion of comprehensive context dramatically improves LLM output quality in clinical applications without extensive data cleaning. By enriching models with data context (field-level metadata, data dictionaries, relational mappings) as well as use case context (semantic data mapping, study design, domain ontologies), we enable flexible natural language exploration while maintaining quality and consistency. This approach bridges the gap between imperfect human queries and precise answers needed for pharmaceutical decision-making, revealing insights within complex, real-world datasets.

title: Agents and MCP and RAG, oh my! Where is the GenAI Yellow-Brick-Road Leading?
abstract: The GenAI landscape has rapidly evolved over the last year in how information can be aggregated and acted upon. Particularly dramatic is the shift to “Agentic” workflows that allow work to be done on behalf of the user or enable LLM applications themselves to do increasingly sophisticated multi-stage actions such as research and code generation and review. This talk will work through our journey and perspectives learned around a shift away from isolated chat based tools (eg chatbots) to more integrated tooling and how we are working to optimize value and efficiency for end users while still maintaining governance and oversight over usage.

title: Customized GenAI coding assistant leveraging multi-agent framework
abstract: We will present a modular, multi-agent coding assistant designed to streamline and enhance the coding experience for clinical insights generation using R packages. Built on a collaborative multi-agent architecture, the system is composed of specialized agents that handle distinct tasks. It intelligently blends publicly available resources with Roche’s internal process knowledge to deliver context-aware code suggestions. An embedded webR environment enables rapid, in-app execution for immediate feedback and iteration. We are currently exploring integration via MCPs to extend the assistant's utility into IDEs such as VSCode and Positron, ensuring seamless support across the developer workflow.

title: Break
Inside an AI Project: From Idea to Value
abstract: Turning an AI idea into real business value isn’t easy. This talk breaks down the key steps in an AI project, how to define its impact, and common challenges—with tips on how to overcome them.

title: Natural Language to Code: AI-Powered Automation for CDISC-Compliant Datasets
abstract: This talk introduces a generative AI-powered system that converts natural language coding specifications into R programs used to generate CDISC-compliant datasets, significantly reducing development time while ensuring compliance and accuracy. Leveraging techniques such as prompt engineering and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), the session will delve into the system’s technical architecture, key lessons learned, and its potential to transform clinical data programming.

title: Considerations of LLM’s benefits and risks
abstract: LLMs in recent years have become immensely popular due to their ability to generate and understand text, images, audio, and video. In this talk, we will discuss the advantages of LLMs while also being mindful of their limitations and risks.

title: Positron Assistant for Developing Shiny Apps
abstract: This talk will explore building AI Apps with a focus on Positron Assistant for Shiny developer experience and in-IDE tooling for accelerating app creation. This talk will discuss tools like ellmer / chatlas / querychat / shinychat and compare it to Positron Assistant.

title: Wrap Up / Q&A
Flexible Clinical Trial Design, Simulation, and Analysis with the R Package rpact
abstract: In this workshop we will explore the capabilities of the validated open-source R package 'rpact', which is available on CRAN and GitHub. rpact is a comprehensive validated, open source, free-of-charge R software package for clinical trial planning, design simulation, and data analysis. rpact is under continuous full-time development since 2017, and comprehensive documentation is available at www.rpact.org. We will provide an introduction to the package and illustrate the usage by several examples. The focus of the package is on group sequential and adaptive designs with p-value combination tests, but also fixed sample designs can be considered. The software can specifically be used to assess design characteristics of popular group sequential designs. However, going beyond those, adaptive designs are a strength of rpact Adaptive multi-armed and population enrichment designs that are based on closed combination tests can be assessed by simulation. The application of the designs for simulation, real data, and estimation is possible for continuous, binary, survival, and count data. Furthermore, we introduce 'RPACT Cloud', a user-friendly platform designed to simplify and enhance the process of clinical trial design and simulations for researchers and practitioners. A free version of RPACT Cloud is available at https//cloud.rpact.com/ and workshop participants will be able to try out the software themselves following the workshop.

title: Debugging Stan Programs
abstract: Having trouble getting your Stan models to behave? This hands-on workshop will explore practical strategies for debugging Stan code, from identifying non-identifiable parameters to improving runtime performance. Participants will gain tools and intuition for building more robust models—skills that extend to a wide range of statistical and stochastic programming tasks.Prerequisite Familiarity with Stan is recommended.

title: Introduction to building (better) R packages
abstract: There are many benefits to turning your R scripts or functions into a package, like making your code easier to re-use, easier to share with others, easier to document, and easier to test. But the process of writing a package can feel intimidating, especially if you haven't done it before. But it doesn't need to! In this interactive workshop, we'll discuss* What things you need to make a package and how to create them* How to write functions (in a package-friendly way) and add them to a package* How to write documentation and examples for functions* Best practices for package development* How to share your package with other people* Useful resources. By the end of this workshop, you will have made an R package! The session aims to be introductory, so you don't need any previous experience of building R packages (or even writing functions!) but some basic knowledge of R will be useful. If you're already a seasoned R package developer, you're also welcome to attend and hopefully you'll still pick up a few package development tips!

title: Getting Started with LLM APIs in R
abstract: LLMs are transforming how we write code, build tools, and analyze data, but getting started with directly working with LLM APIs can feel daunting. This workshop will introduce participants to programming with LLM APIs in R using ellmer, an open-source package that makes it easy to work with LLMs from R. We’ll cover the basics of calling LLMs from R, as well as system prompt design, tool calling, and building basic chatbots. No AI or machine learning background is required—just basic R familiarity. Participants will leave with example scripts they can adapt to their own projects.

title: Hands on with Cardinal: Harmonizing Clinical Reporting with Open‑Source TLGs
abstract: Cardinal is an open-source collection of standardized table, listing, and graph (TLG) templates designed to streamline the process of clinical output review, comparison, and meta-analysis—promoting efficient communication to stakeholders while aligning with CDISC’s ARD/ARM efforts. In this workshop, we’ll introduce the  gtsummary  package for table creation and walk through Cardinal’s growing catalog of TLGs. Participants will get hands-on experience generating key outputs—ideally working on examples that are directly relevant to your own work. Whether you're new to Cardinal, looking to integrate it into your own workflow, or interested in contributing to the project, this workshop will provide practical insights and real-world applications for modern clinical reporting.

title: Opening Remarks
Open-Source Culture and Data Strategy in SHIONOGI: A New Value-Creation Model for Pharma
abstract: For pharmaceutical companies, effective use of data is a critical source of competitiveness. This keynote introduces Shionogi’s data strategy and organizational transformation centered on open-source adoption. By standardizing R/Python-based analytics, fostering cross-functional knowledge sharing, and ensuring reproducibility, we have achieved both efficiency and transparency. The talk will further highlight our governance framework aligned with regulatory requirements and our collaborations with the open-source community, presenting a forward-looking vision for sustainable data-driven innovation in pharma.

title: Strategically Assisting Statistical programmers To succeed in R (SAS2R)
abstract: In the Life Science Industry, there has been activity over the last few years to embrace Open-Source languages (mainly R) for performing activities which have traditionally been done in SAS. This talk will focus on effective strategies for teaching statistical programmers with experience using SAS in their daily work (SDTM/ADaM/TFL, etc.) how to learn and transition to R. This strategy consists of four key components. The first focuses on the statistical programmer’s prior experience with R–ranging from no exposure at all, to having used it before entering the industry, to maintaining ongoing familiarity. The second component considers the environmental resources available within the company, such as existing R learning materials and whether generative AI tools have been introduced to support the learning process. The Third component reviews the timing of R-related tasks and works backward to determine which aspect to focus on–basic syntax, pharmaverse packages, or task-specific skills. This helps prevent both knowledge decay from inactivity and overload that hinders learning. The final component involves practical exercises where learners reproduce deliverables previously generated in SAS using R. This approach helps bridge the gap between R syntax and practical application, while fostering a sense of achievement through successful replication.

title: Side-by-side by Design: Pharma Data Handling with Merge, Join, Match, and Hash in R
abstract: In this session, a organizer from the SAS Users Group Japan explores comprehensive strategies for key-based data integration with R, emphasizing practical comparisons between methods. Attendees will gain insights into the differences and similarities between SAS Merge, SQL Joins, Base R merging , dplyr joins, as well as advanced R tools such as the hash package and rtables. Additionally, the presentation includes specific discussions on data merging practices relevant to CDISC standards, including examples from ADaM and SDTM datasets.

title: Risk Assessment Deep Dive
abstract: It is important to set-up validation strategy of analysis systems in drug development in pharmaceutical industry. One of the hot topics in open source software(OSS) utilization in this space is R package validation. Risk-based approach of the validation is commonly employed. In this presentation, we summarize the available tools (e.g. riskmetric, etc.) for risk assessment in the approach and discuss the points to consider. This is a presentation by phuse Japan open source technology WG.

title: Break
Leverage template-based automated reporting on DMC materials preparation
abstract: Preparing Data Monitoring Committee (DMC) materials is a critical yet often time-consuming task in clinical trial safety oversight. Traditional workflows, relying heavily on manual copy-pasting across multiple documents, introduce inefficiencies and increase the risk of errors. We present a flexible, template-based automated reporting workflow using R Markdown and the  flextable  package to efficiently generate commonly used tables, figures, and listings in Word or slide formats with predefined formatting and narrative elements. Starting from a customizable template, users can adjust layout, styling, and perform basic data handling. Rather than enforcing strict automation, this approach emphasizes reproducibility and user control— minimizing manual formatting work and errors while enabling tailored, efficient outputs for review and documentation.

title: Dynamic Creation of Kaplan-Meier Plots and Summary Measure Tables for Survival Data with R Shiny
abstract: Summarization and visualization are essential for interpreting statistical analysis results, but coding programs takes a certain amount of time. However, in interactive discussions, there are situations where it is desirable to understand data/statistical analysis results in a timely manner. In such situations, dynamic summarization and visualization can be expected to promote discussion and speed up decision-making. The statistical analysis software R provides the Shiny package that enables this dynamic activity. In our presentation, we will introduce a method to create dynamic summary tables and Kaplan-Meier plots when subgroup variables and parameters are changed, focusing particularly on survival data, using the Shiny package.

title: autoslideR: Streamlining slide deck generation for clinical reporting events
abstract: The standard process of developing the slide deck for clinical reporting events includes manually populating numbers from static outputs and a separate QC. The process is time-consuming, resource-intensive, and error-prone. To address these issues, we created “autoslideR”, an R package to automate the slide deck generation for multiple clinical reporting events. autoslideR has successfully supported slide creation for several study endorsement meetings, IMC meetings, as well as dose escalation meetings for early development, saving teams 0.5 to 4 days for the slide deck preparation compared to the time it traditionally takes.  This talk explores the key features and technical advantages of autoslideR, such as supporting customized layout creations from existing templates, as well as adding placeholder slides to accelerate final slide preparation.

title: Break
From Harmony to Hybrid: Charting a Practical Course for R Adoption in Pharma
abstract: The journey towards end-to-end (e2e) R-based regulatory submissions is one of the most significant transformations in our industry today. While the technical capabilities of R are clear, achieving success is a complex endeavor that requires more than just good code. This keynote draws inspiration from the classical strategic concept of "天时地利人和" (The Right Time, Place, and People) to frame the challenges and triumphs of this journey, using a successful e2e submission as a guiding case study. Shifting from this framework to practice, we will analyze current R adoption trends across China's pharmaceutical landscape, from SDTM to TLG generation. Data reveals that while R is gaining strong traction in analysis and reporting, its use in foundational stages like SDTM creation remains a challenge. This observation leads to two key discussions first, the pragmatic case for hybrid submissions, leveraging the strengths of both R and SAS, and second, the emerging role of Artificial Intelligence. We will touch upon how the industry is beginning to explore AI to solve complex challenges like SDTM mapping, discussing both the immense opportunities and the practical hurdles ahead.

title: Emerging trend of LLM development in R and implementation
abstract: Recent advancements in R have significantly simplified the integration of large language models (LLMs) into data workflows. This session offers a practical overview of how LLMs can be applied in R through a curated set of tools and packages. We highlight several LLM-related packages that boost productivity, support AI-assisted programming, and enable advanced tools such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Real-world examples and demo are provided to demonstrate practical usage. This session is tailored for R users seeking to enhance their workflows with AI-powered capabilities and help illustrate how current available LLM-related package can work.

title: An R package to consolidate pretest probability models and guidelines for CAD
abstract: Most clinicians in cardiology use an online portal such as HeartScore (https//www.escardio.org/Education/Practice-Tools/CVD-prevention-toolbox/HeartScore) or CAD consortium (https//qxmd.com/calculate/calculator_287/pre-test-probability-of-cad-cad-consortium) to calculate a risk score for a patient.  As risk scores continue to evolve and change overtime, it can be a tedious process to recalculate the risk score of many patients as these online portal could only do so one patient at a time.  While there are R package such as CVrisk (https//cran.r-project.org/web/packages/CVrisk/index.html), RiskScorescvd (https//cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RiskScorescvd/index.html) and preventR (https//cran.r-project.org/web/packages/preventr/index.html) dedicated to calculating a patient’s risk of having cardiovascular disease (stroke, heart attack), there is no R package that is dedicated to calculating pretest risk scores for obstructive CAD.  Pretest score for CAD are more useful than risk score for cardiovascular diseases (stroke, heart attack) as early detection and intervention treatment of CAD can lead to better outcomes.  An R package called pretestcad (https//cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pretestcad/index.html) was made to fill this gap, allowing users to calculate these scores () automatically for many patients, prior to deciding if the patient should go for CT scan or invasive coronary angiography to confirm  Examples of such scores are the 2017 PROMISE Minimal-Risk Score and the 2020 Winther et. al. Risk-Factor-weighted Clinical Likelihood (RF-CL) and Coronary Artery Calcium Score-Weighted Clinical Likelihood (CACS-CL) PTP which was recommended to be used in the 2024 ESC Guidelines (https//academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/36/3415/7743115).

title: Enhancing Efficiency in e-CRT Creation for PMDA Through R Shiny App Development Using Vibe Coding
abstract: At the workshop hosted by JPMA (DS, KT3) on June 25, 2025, a survey was conducted regarding inquiries on e-Data submitted to PMDA. Results from the survey revealed that the most common inquiries were related to inconsistencies in documentation, such as differences in the MedDRA version and WHO-DD version listed in the Reviewer's Guide and Define.xml, as well as omissions regarding the presence of SUPPxx domains. To address these inconsistencies, I created an R Shiny app by Vibe Coding using ChatGPT to check for inconsistencies across documents. Despite being a beginner in R, I successfully developed an app to resolve these issues efficiently. This presentation shares the insights gained from the development process. Additionally, beyond creating e-CRT packages, I hope this example serves as a reference for utilizing Vibe Coding (not limited to R Shiny but potentially using Python or other tools) to develop apps that streamline workflows and improve efficiency in one's daily tasks.

title: {meRlin} - context-aware AI assistant for clinical programming
abstract: In highly regulated environments where clinical data confidentiality is paramount, traditional AI coding assistants like ChatGPT present two significant challenges they require data exposure to external systems, and they lack context-specific knowledge of organizational data structures and standards. We present an innovative solution that bridges this gap a secure, context-aware application that combines large language models (LLMs) with clinical data standards to assist R users in analyzing confidential healthcare data. Our package, built using the open-source project  gptstudio  and Apollo (an internal qualified LLM service) and deployed on Posit Workbench, has the ability to reference our organization’s clinical data standards and other internal documentation. This enables it to generate and execute R code that is precisely tailored to our data structures, variable definitions, and analytical requirements. The system can help the user perform various tasks including exploratory data analysis, data quality checks, putting together a first draft for a  teal  or DaVinci Shiny application, as well as generate TLGs for clinical reporting.  We will demonstrate how this tool serves dual purposes accelerating the work of experienced R programmers while simultaneously functioning as an educational platform for R learners working with clinical data. Unlike generic AI coding assistants, our solution provides contextually relevant code suggestions that align with organizational standards and practices, all while maintaining data privacy and regulatory compliance. This presentation will showcase real-world applications, discuss the technical architecture, and explore how similar systems could be implemented in other organizations working with sensitive data.

title: Advanced Clinical Reporting with officer and flextable
abstract: In this workshop you will be working with the officer and flextable packages to create sophisticated clinical reports in Word format using R with a reproducible approach. Going from clinical data all the way through to complete pharmaceutical report generation. Specifically, we will walk through an end-to-end example focusing on advanced document structure management, complex table creation following pharmaceutical standards, and integration of ggplot2 visualizations. The workshop is divided into two parts first, discovering the fundamentals of officer and flextable packages, then moving to advanced clinical reporting techniques including section management, headers and footers customization, and cross-reference handling for complete pharmaceutical report composition.

title: Creating Polished, Branded Documents with Quarto
abstract: Join us for a hands-on, one-day workshop at R/Phama, where we’ll explore the versatility of Quarto output formats. You will learn how to create dynamic websites, professional PDF documents, engaging presentations, and interactive dashboards using Quarto. This workshop highlights Quarto's powerful theming capabilities, including the new support for brand.yml, which ensures that your work maintains a professional and cohesive style across all formats.

title: Polars: The Blazing Fast Python Framework for Modern Clinical Trial Data Exploration
abstract: Clinical trials generate complex and standards driven datasets that can slow down traditional data processing tools. This workshop introduces Polars, a cutting-edge Python DataFrame library engineered with a high-performance backend and the Apache Arrow columnar format for blazingly fast data manipulation. Attendees will learn how Polars lays the foundation for the pharmaverse-py, streamlining the data clinical workflow from database querying and complex data wrangling to the potential task of prepping data for regulatory Tables, Figures, and Listings (TFLs). Discover the 'delightful' Polars API and how its speed dramatically accelerates both exploratory and regid data tasks in pharmaceutical drug development. The workshop is led by Michael Chow, a Python developer at Posit who is a key contributor to open-source data tools, notably helping to launch the data presentation library Great Tables, and focusing on bringing efficient data analysis patterns to Python.

title: How to use pointblank to understand, validate, and document your data
abstract: This workshop will focus on the data quality and data documentation workflows that the pointblank package makes possible. We will use functions that allow us to (1) quickly understand a new dataset (2) validate tabular data using rules that are based on our understanding of the data (3) fully document a table by describing its variables and other important details. The pointblank package was created to scale from small validation problems (“Let’s make certain this table fits my expectations before moving on”) to very large (“Let’s validate these 35 database tables every day and ensure data quality is maintained”) and we’ll delve into all sorts of data quality scenarios so you’ll be comfortable using this package in your organization. Data documentation is seemingly and unfortunately less common in organizations (maybe even less than the practice of data validation). We’ll learn all about how this doesn’t have to be a tedious chore. The pointblank package allows you to create informative and beautiful data documentation that will help others understand what’s in all those tables that are so vital to an organization.

title: Opening Remarks
Improving precision healthcare for under-represented and genetically diverse global populations
abstract: Precision healthcare holds immense potential to transform disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment by tailoring care to an individual’s genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors. The majority of genomics research however, has been focused on populations of European ancestry, leaving under-represented and genetically diverse global populations, such as Indigenous Australians, underserved. This gap limits the generalisability of biomedical insights and exacerbates existing health inequities, but also limits the utility of language models that may have a significant impact on the way that genetic variants can be prioritised for drug discovery. In this talk, I describe some of the challenges associated with the analysis of Indigenous Australian genomes and discuss approaches that our team are using to develop precision approaches for primary healthcare in Australia.

title: Break
Exploring AI tools in clinical trial data analysis
abstract: Nowadays, with the development of AI technology, proficiency in using AI tools has become an indispensable skill. The topic expresses how, as a beginner, to utilize AI tools to solve the challenges actually encountered in clinical trials and save programmers' resources. As well as the common principles that should be followed when using AI tools summarized in the process.  In this presentation, hands-on experience to decrease 80% of resource during exploratory analysis using Cursor and Claude 4.0 will be shared.

title: An R Package cgmguru for Automated Glycemic Event Detection From Continuous Glucose Monitoring Data
abstract: The high volume of Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) data presents a significant bottleneck for large-scale clinical research. To address this computational challenge, we developed cgmguru, an R package that utilizes Rcpp to seamlessly integrate R and C++ for high-performance processing. The cgmguru package calculates established CGM consensus metrics, including level 1/2 and extended hyper- and hypoglycemic events, based on CGM consensus statement for clinical trials. Furthermore, the package implements a novel algorithm for detecting post-prandial peak glucose, based on the Glucose Rate Increase Detector (GRID) algorithm. This detection method has been successfully applied in clinical research. In this session, I will introduce how CGM research is used in the pharmaceutical industry. I will also demonstrate how the cgmguru package can be used in both clinical trials and observational studies.

title: Break
Interactive and Reproducible Reports with Quarto
abstract: In this session, I’ll explore how Quarto can be used to create dynamic, interactive reports for pharma research and development. I’ll show how to integrate Observable JS for real-time data exploration and visualization, while incorporating plots from both R and Python into a single, cohesive report. Using Quarto’s multi-language support, I’ll demonstrate how to combine R’s power with Python’s capabilities seamlessly. A key highlight will be the CloseRead extension, a custom Quarto format that enables scrollytelling features in HTML documents. With CloseRead, I’ll showcase how to build interactive narratives that make your reports more engaging and easier to understand. Whether you're presenting clinical trial data or drug discovery insights, Quarto offers an innovative way to tell your data story. Whether it’s regulatory reports, progress summaries, or even model results, Quarto’s flexibility can save time and reduce errors. Join me to see how we can make pharma reporting more efficient, transparent, and open.

title: Using Analysis Results Data using {cards} for PMDA Oncology inqueries
abstract: In clinical drug development, regulatory agencies like Japan’s Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Agency (PMDA) often issue data inquiries that require many additional analyses, especially in oncology trials. These requests demand the rapid generation of multiple reports.  We propose using the R package  cards  to create Analysis Results Datasets (ARD) that standardize adverse event summary outputs. The ARD concept provides a structured, reusable format for reporting analysis results. By defining ARDs for PMDA oncology queries, we can aggregate events (e.g., all adverse events, Grade ≥3, fatal, serious, or those leading to treatment modifications) in a unified way. This standardization enables more efficient processing, easier reuse of analysis code, and improved quality control. We will introduce the ARD framework and demonstrate a new ARD-based analysis workflow using  cards . Our results show that this approach accelerates report generation, ensures consistency across analyses, and supports future extensions of the workflow.

title: Reach for R Low Hanging Fruit for Faster Results
abstract: With the pharma industry expanding packages within pharmaverse, is your organization ready to reach for R low hanging fruit for faster results? This presentation will show how R packages and functions are ‘out of the box’ production ready for fast results without having to invest in SAS silo resources or expenses. While some R mentoring is required to understand key differences with SAS and R fundamental concepts, smarter organizations can get a jump start on their submission ready deliverables. R packages in data management and graphs enable ‘plug-n-play’ queries and plots. The R packages used to create the Clinical Study Report (CSR) tables and lists offer R script templates that can be customized. CDISC submission support packages include the define.xml and tidyCDISC. Finally, popular pharmaverse packages rtables, admiral and teal will also be featured.

title: Break
MedxR Package - Bridging Regulatory Drug Data from the FDA and Health Canada into R
abstract: In this talk, I will introduce MedxR, a new R package that connects directly to public regulatory APIs from the U.S. FDA and Health Canada. MedxR allows users to programmatically search, retrieve, and analyze drug approval data, recall alerts, product labels, and ingredient information. This tool is designed to support pharmacovigilance, drug research, academic use, and real-world data analysis in regulatory science. I will demonstrate key functions such as querying drug products, tracking recalls, and comparing medication records across both agencies

title: risk.assessr:  extending its use in the package validation process
abstract: The Sanofi R Validation team is currently creating a number of cutting edge GitHub processes to employ the risk.assessr package to help Sanofi effectively manage risks associated with internal, third-party and open-source packages.    The first process is a database to store the risk metric data (RCMD check, test coverage, documentation metrics, traceability matrix), create Sanofi risk thresholds, and generate documentation for package acceptance/rejection for the team to make a decision about a target package. The process also populates the documentation with any metrics that do not pass the Sanofi criteria.   Next is a GitHub CICD process to run risk.assessr on an individual target package for a specific package evaluation and store that data in the DB.
